issues.legal_issue: A land-acquisition law unrelated to agrarian reform is not protected as a law concerning agrarian reform.
material_facts: The challenged law authorised acquisition of both urban and agricultural land for works connected with flood control or prevention of erosion.
Acquired land did not need to be an estate or part of an estate, and the law had no connection with agrarian reform, land tenures, or the elimination of intermediaries.
issues.conclusion: The law was not protected by Article 31A because it was not a law concerning agrarian reform.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws concerning agrarian reform, not every law that acquires land. The Court relied on Kochuni v. State of Madras, [1960] 3 SCR 887; Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, [1965] 1 SCR 82; and P. V. Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Madras, [1965] 1 SCR 641.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorising the acquisition of land.
predicates.flood_control_acquisition: The law authorised land acquisition for works or measures connected with flood control or prevention of erosion.
predicates.agrarian_reform_measure: The law formed part of agrarian reform, including reform of land tenures or elimination of intermediaries.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition law is directed to flood-control works and is not an agrarian-reform measure, it is not protected as agrarian reform.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional exception for promoting public health or preventing danger to life or property does not protect a law authorising permanent acquisition of property.
material_facts: The law permanently vested acquired land in the State for flood-control and erosion-prevention works.
The State relied on the purpose of preventing danger to life or property to claim protection from the compensation requirement.
The Court distinguished permanent acquisition from destruction, impairment, requisition, or temporary occupation strictly necessary to abate a public menace.
issues.conclusion: The law was a law for acquisition of property, not a law for preventing danger to life or property, and was not protected by Article 31(5)(b)(ii).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(5)(b)(ii), read in the context of Article 31 before and after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, does not exempt permanent acquisition from Article 31(2). It may protect laws providing for destruction or temporary occupation strictly necessary to abate a public menace. The Court considered State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose, [1954] SCR 587, and Dwarkadas Shrinivas of Bombay v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., [1954] SCR 674.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_law: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorising the State to take private property.
predicates.permanent_state_acquisition: The law permanently transferred the property or its ownership to the State rather than authorising only temporary occupation or a temporary taking.
predicates.public_safety_purpose: The acquisition was intended to promote public health or prevent danger to life or property.

issues.definition: When a challenged law permanently transfers property to the State for a public-safety purpose, the public-safety exception does not cover that acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-amendment acquisition law violates the compensation requirement when its prescribed compensation does not ensure a just equivalent of the property taken.
material_facts: The acquisition law predated the constitutional amendment that changed Article 31(2), so its validity was judged under Article 31(2) as it then stood.
For land, the law capped compensation at a fixed multiple of annual land revenue, although land values had increased substantially since revenue assessments were made.
For buildings or structures, the law based compensation on the sale proceeds of their materials plus an additional percentage, rather than their value as buildings or structures at acquisition.
The State did not show that these measures bore a relation to market value or ensured a just equivalent of the property taken.
issues.conclusion: The law did not ensure payment of a just equivalent of the property appropriated and violated Article 31(2) as it stood before the Fourth Amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, the principles for determining compensation had to ensure a just equivalent of the property taken. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, [1954] SCR 558, and State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, [1964] 6 SCR 936.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_pre_amendment_acquisition_law and compensation_capped_by_old_revenue_assessment and building_payment_based_on_materials and not state_shows_just_equivalent

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_pre_amendmen: A party challenged an acquisition law enacted before a constitutional change to the applicable compensation requirement.
predicates.compensation_capped_by_old_revenue_asses: The law capped land compensation by reference to revenue assessments that did not reflect the land's value at acquisition.
predicates.building_payment_based_on_materials: The law measured compensation for a building or structure by the value of its materials rather than its value as a building or structure.
predicates.state_shows_just_equivalent: The State demonstrated that the statutory compensation measures ensured a just equivalent of the property taken.

issues.definition: When a challenged pre-amendment acquisition law uses outdated revenue-based caps and materials-based building payments, and the State does not show that those measures provide a just equivalent, the law fails the applicable compensation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition law violates equal protection when it gives differently compensated treatment to similarly situated landowners without a reasonable relation to the object of acquisition.
material_facts: The general land-acquisition law permitted acquisition for public purposes with compensation based on market value, while the special law permitted acquisition for flood-control and erosion-prevention works using a different and substantially lower compensation method.
Landowners could lose land to the State under either law, but the purpose of acquisition did not provide a reasonable basis for the different treatment.
The Court rejected the classification between land acquired for flood-control purposes and land acquired for other public purposes as unrelated to the object of acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The special acquisition law violated Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification and differential treatment only where substantial differences bear a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court relied on P. V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, [1965] 1 SCR 614, which held that differential acquisition and compensation treatment for land acquired under different laws could violate Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law governing the acquisition of land.
predicates.similarly_situated_landowners_face_diffe: Landowners in materially similar circumstances receive different compensation treatment because their land is acquired under different legal regimes.
predicates.classification_lacks_relation_to_acquisi: The difference in treatment has no reasonable relation to the object of acquiring the land for the State.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition law treats similarly situated landowners differently in compensation without a reasonable relation to the acquisition object, it violates equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: A validating law that depends on deeming acquisitions under an unconstitutional earlier law cannot validate those acquisitions.
material_facts: The later law deemed certain land taken before it came into force to have been acquired under the earlier acquisition law.
Its compensation, award, and other ancillary provisions relied on the earlier law, and its central deeming provision was the basis for treating the acquisitions as valid.
The earlier acquisition law was unconstitutional and had no legal existence.
issues.conclusion: The later law was invalid because its deemed acquisitions and ancillary provisions depended on the unconstitutional earlier law; the legislature could not validate acquisitions made under that law.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature cannot make an acquisition valid by deeming it to have been made under a constitutionally invalid law. Where a later law's core deeming provision depends on that earlier law, the later law's ancillary provisions fall with it and cannot be enforced.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validating_l: A party challenged the validity of a law intended to validate earlier land acquisitions.
predicates.underlying_acquisition_law_invalid: The earlier law under which the acquisitions are deemed to have occurred was held unconstitutional.
predicates.later_law_depends_on_underlying_law: The later law's central deeming provision and its ancillary acquisition or compensation provisions depend on the earlier law.

issues.definition: When a challenged validating law depends on an earlier acquisition law that is unconstitutional, the validating law is invalid.
